scams.name: The Nakasu Girls Bar ¥1,000,000 Overcharge
scams.description: Street hustlers lure visitors into girls bars in Nakasu where hostesses continuously serve drinks without quoting prices. Bills escalate dramatically—documented cases range from ¥400,000 to over ¥1,000,000 for three hours. Bouncers block exits when customers question charges. Some venues have yakuza affiliations.
scams.avoidance: Never follow street hustlers into Nakasu venues. Patronize only Google Maps-listed establishments with 4.5+ stars and 50+ English reviews. Demand printed menus with prices before ordering. Leave immediately if seated without pricing information. Call 110 if pressured, citing Fukuoka's Bottakuri Prevention Ordinance.

scams.name: The Nakasu Yatai Foreign-Tourist Overcharge
scams.description: Riverside yatai food stalls systematically overcharge foreign tourists while charging local prices to Japanese customers. A ¥3,200 order becomes ¥5,600. Reviews confirm this targeting pattern is widespread and deliberate, with locals avoiding these tourist-facing stalls.
scams.avoidance: Eat at Tenjin yatai instead, particularly Nagahama. Photograph menus before sitting. Refuse stalls where hustlers recruited you from the street. Demand itemized receipts before paying. Prioritize stalls with 4.5+ star ratings from Japanese reviewers.
scams.location: Nakasu riverside yatai along Naka River

scams.name: The Hakata Station Tsukushi-guchi Hustler Shakedown
scams.description: Organized hustler groups operate at Hakata Station's east exit, approaching visitors with low-price drink offers (quoted as ¥3,000) that balloon to ¥15,000–30,000. Hustlers earn 10–20% commission per customer. Inside venues, unrequested appetizers and service charges are added. Top earners pull ¥500,000 monthly.
scams.avoidance: Use Hakata-guchi (west) exit instead. Ignore all hustlers—avoid eye contact and engagement. Select restaurants on Google Maps or Tabelog before arriving. Call 110 if pressured. Note that Fukuoka posted anti-kyakuhiki warning signs at Tsukushi-guchi since 2020.

scams.name: The Tinder / Matching App Bar Lure
scams.description: Users matching on Tinder or Bumble with women who suggest meeting at specific Nakasu or Tenjin bars encounter massive bills (¥40,000–80,000 for minimal drinks and food). The woman is paid per delivered customer and typically vanishes before the bill arrives. Named venues include PIGLET bar on the 3rd floor of Yamamoto Building near Nakasukawabata Station.
scams.avoidance: Insist on venues you select from Google Maps with visible street presence and 4.5+ reviews. Unmatch if she refuses your suggestion. Suggest daytime coffee or walks before drinks. Leave if warning signs appear (upper floor, no signage, she knows staff). Screenshot named problematic venues to pattern-match.
scams.location: Nakasu and Tenjin bars accessed via dating apps

scams.name: The Booking.com 'Cash in the Fridge' Rental Scam
scams.description: You book an apartment near Hakata Station on Booking.com for around ¥18,000 a night and pay in full. The night before check-in, the host messages you on LINE — not through Booking.com — with an apology: '¥50,500 cleaning deposit wasn't added to the listing; please leave it in an envelope inside the refrigerator when you arrive, or the door code won't work.' The property is a converted 1LDK in a multi-tenant building with no name on the intercom. The deposit is never refunded, Booking.com has no chat record because everything moved to LINE, and the operator is usually running an unlicensed Minpaku in violation of Japan's Private Lodging Business Act.
scams.avoidance: Keep every message inside the Booking.com or Airbnb chat. Any host who moves the conversation to LINE, WhatsApp, or email and then asks for extra cash is running a scam — report the listing through the platform's 'report listing' flow and refuse to pay. Booking.com and Airbnb will refund you if you never paid the cash and will investigate if you did. For stays of three nights or more in Fukuoka, prefer hotels over Minpaku: Hotel Forza Hakata-guchi and Richmond Hotel Hakata Ekimae are both under ¥15,000 a night and fully licensed.
scams.location: Short-term rentals near Hakata Station (south side)

scams.name: The Hakata Station Phishing Approach
scams.description: You've just stepped off the Shinkansen at Hakata Station with a roller bag in each hand. A friendly man in a lanyard steps up: 'Tourism survey — can I photograph your passport for the visitor count?' The lanyard is homemade, the badge is a laminated print, and the 'survey' is a data harvest. Within 48 hours, either someone calls your hotel impersonating you and talks the front desk into your folio, or unfamiliar charges appear on the card you linked to your passport at check-in. A common variant waits at the taxi stand: a man in a suit quotes ¥8,000 flat to your hotel instead of the metered ¥1,500 fare, and once you're belted in, he extends the route through Kego.
scams.avoidance: Never hand your passport to anyone who isn't in uniform behind a desk. If someone asks for passport details or your hotel name on the platform or in the taxi rank, say 'sumimasen' and walk to the nearest uniformed station attendant — one is posted at the central Chikushi-guchi exit at almost all hours. From the airport, take the Fukuoka City Subway Kuko Line (¥270, five minutes to Hakata) instead of a taxi. At the taxi rank itself, board only cars in the official queue with green license plates, and ignore anyone who approaches you directly.
scams.location: Hakata Station and Fukuoka Airport taxi stands
